### 2026-09-12 · 🚨 FIXED — a code commit with a docs commit on top of it has never deployed, and tonight it ate the sentinel change (#97) · Cowork cloud

**Shipped:** `vercel.json` (the deploy gate's comparison base), `__tests__/deploy-gate-compares-against-the-last-deployed-commit.test.ts`, `docs/reference/known-issues.md` (**new #97, closed**). Revert: `git revert` the commit whose message starts `fix(deploy): compare against the last DEPLOYED commit`.

**🚨 FOUND BY CHECKING, NOT BY ALARM — AND IT HAD ALREADY SWALLOWED TONIGHT'S WORK.** After pushing the sentinel ack-mode + cadence-arm commit with a docs commit stacked on top, I read the Vercel deployment list rather than assuming: the production deployment for the tip was **`CANCELED`, with the route unshipped.** ⭐ **Vercel builds the PUSH, not each commit**, so `ignoreCommand`'s `git diff --quiet HEAD^ HEAD -- . ':(exclude)docs/**' …` ran exactly once against the TIP — **a docs-only tip skipped the build and took the code commit underneath it down with it.** Green CI, a real deployment row, nothing live.

**⚠ THE THIRD OCCURRENCE, AND THE FIRST TWO WERE ANSWERED WITH A HABIT.** CLAUDE.md already records this biting twice, with the standing remedy *push code last*. ⛔ **A habit is not a fix** — it fails exactly when a session is long or interrupted, which is when it is needed, and it cannot cover the adjacent shapes (a build skipped for another reason, a reverted deploy, several pushes between builds).

**✅ THE FIX IS THE BASE, NOT THE EXCLUSIONS.** The gate now diffs against **`VERCEL_GIT_PREVIOUS_SHA`** — Vercel's own SHA of the **last successful deployment**, exposed precisely when an Ignored Build Step is configured — so the question is *has anything non-docs changed since what is actually LIVE*, which is push-shape-independent. ⛔ **It degrades to `HEAD^` on an empty variable or a sha missing from the shallow clone, never to "skip"**: the cost of guessing wrong here is shipping nothing, silently. The `:(exclude)` pathspecs are untouched, so the sibling `deploy-and-ci-agree-on-what-docs-means` guard still holds.

**⭐ PINNED BY BEHAVIOUR, WITH THE BUG ITSELF AS THE CONTROL.** The real `ignoreCommand` is executed by `bash` against throwaway git repos: the exact shape that shipped nothing must now BUILD, **and the same test asserts that the old `HEAD^` base skips it** — so the test would have failed before the fix, which is the only version of a regression test worth having. A genuinely docs-only push since the live deployment is still skipped; the saving is not given back.

**⚠ THE FIX SHIPPED BROKEN ONCE, AND THE WAY IT FAILED IS THE BEST EVIDENCE FOR IT.** `ignoreCommand` is capped at **256 characters** by Vercel's schema, and an over-long one rejects the **whole `vercel.json`** — `crons` included — with the deployment in state `ERROR`. ⭐ **The new base is what surfaced it on its own first push:** the docs-tipped push BUILT (as designed), the build failed loudly on the schema, and production stayed on the last good deployment. **Under the old `HEAD^` rule that push would have been skipped and a broken `vercel.json` would have sat on `main` until some later code push discovered it.** ✅ Logic moved to `scripts/vercel-ignore-build.sh`; `ignoreCommand` is now a 35-character call; the cap is pinned by test. ⛔ **And both gate tests were re-pointed at the SCRIPT — the sibling `deploy-and-ci-agree-on-what-docs-means` would otherwise have extracted zero pathspecs and PASSED VACUOUSLY**, retiring itself in silence. Its extractor now throws on an empty set.

**⚠ WHAT IT DOES NOT FIX:** a long red streak widens the diff window rather than narrowing it, because the base stays at the last *successful* deploy. That is the safe direction, and it is stated so a large post-outage build is not read as a bug.

**⭐⭐ AND THE TRADE IS NOW MEASURED RATHER THAN ARGUED, WITH A REPLAY THAT VALIDATES ITSELF.** Both rules were run against the real tree for **60 consecutive production pushes** (9.6 h, multi-session): **OLD 35 builds · NEW 38 · 0 dropped.** ✅ **"35" is not a model output — the window holds exactly 35 `READY` deployments**, so the old-rule replay lands on the record it is replaying; the 36th real build is the `ERROR` that already ran under the new rule. 🚨 **The three pushes the new rule adds are one-for-one the bug:** `de0c8b3`, **`55f8055` (tonight's sentinel commit)** and `1564788` (the push that surfaced the 256-char cap — under the old rule a broken `vercel.json` would have sat on `main` unbuilt). ⭐ **So the rate is not "three times ever" but 3 of 60 — about one push in twenty shipping nothing.** ⚠ **Cost, filed to #61: +8.6 % on build count, nothing saved back**, and the window is dense enough that the ratio transfers while the absolute rate does not.

grep; a static check for `&& teamHref &&` would pin a spelling. Left uncovered on
purpose, noted for e2e.

That one character is the whole defect: an overflowing line WRAPS, and two ~12px lines centred in a 13px box are both sliced through the middle. ⚠ **A wrong number reaching the same conclusion is the most expensive kind, because nothing ever forces it to be re-derived** — it had already been copied into three places before I checked it.

**The live instance, named:** `jamesdillonbond`'s slot 5 is Disney Pinnacle's `" Walt Disney Animation Studios • The Lion King Vol.2"` — **51 characters, the longest set name any pinned trophy carries** (next is 31).

**Shipped the measurement rather than a tuned constant.** `captionCharBudget(w) = max(12, floor(w / 5.7))`, and the new guard **reads the TTF and re-derives the advance** rather than restating it: it asserts the face really is monospace (191/194 share one advance — a proportional font would make "characters per pixel" meaningless and every other assertion vacuous), reads the rendered `fontSize`/`letterSpacing` **out of the route source** so it cannot drift from the JSX, and then checks every tile width the card can produce. ⭐ **Controls in BOTH directions, each proven by mutation: `5.6` fails the fit case, `5.9` fails the TIGHTNESS case** (one more character must NOT fit at the two live widths — without that the guard passes for a budget of one character). Plus a floor check, so the `max(12, …)` can never be silently doing the work.

**Same class, second surface: the profile card's serial strip had no width and no overflow at all.** It fits today — the widest live serial+tier pair is 20 characters, 120px in a 130px tile — but measured over every moment anyone actually holds, the longest serial line is **18 characters and the longest tier 10**, which is 28 × 5.8 + the 4px gap = **166px inside a 130px six-slab tile**. Now `maxWidth` + `nowrap` + `overflow: hidden`; nothing visible changes today and the spill is structurally impossible.

**Three promotions, and CLAUDE.md was at 39,943 of 40,000 so one had to DISPLACE.** (1) 🚨 **`CREATE OR REPLACE` IS A FULL-BODY WRITE — RE-READ THE LIVE OBJECT IMMEDIATELY BEFORE ONE** is now a CLAUDE.md database bullet, paid for by displacing the `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW` reloptions bullet **verbatim** into `database.md` (they are the same lesson at two objects) and condensing the `check_*` shapes bullet to its pointer, whose long form also moved verbatim. File is now **39,964** — re-measured with `node -e` + `.length`, never `wc -c`. ### 2026-09-12 · ✅ CODE — two files decide whether a push deploys and whether its tests run, in two syntaxes, and nothing tied them together; plus #61's biggest lever is now sized at 26.7% of builds · Claude Code cloud, Trevor: "keep going"

**Shipped:** `__tests__/deploy-and-ci-agree-on-what-docs-means.test.ts` (new), `docs/reference/known-issues.md` (#61). Revert: `git revert` the commit whose message starts `test(ci): pin the deploy gate and the CI classifier`. **Test-only — no route, config or DB change.**

**⭐ THE GAP.** `vercel.json`'s `ignoreCommand` decides whether **production deploys**, using `:(exclude)docs/** *.md *.mdx` pathspecs. `ci.yml`'s `changes` job decides whether the **ten code jobs run**, using `grep -vE '^docs/|\.md$|\.mdx$'`. **Same question, two files, two syntaxes, no link.** They agree today and nothing would have said so if they stopped.

**⛔ The dangerous direction is asymmetric and it is the one nobody would notice: CI wider than Vercel means the code jobs SKIP and production DEPLOYS ANYWAY** — untested code live. The reverse (Vercel wider) means code merges green and never ships, which CLAUDE.md records as having **bitten twice**.

**🚨 AND THIS WAS ABOUT TO MATTER, which is why it got built now rather than filed.** #61 proposes widening the deploy-side exclusions. Whoever does that edits `vercel.json` — one obvious file — and the hand-copied regex in a different file silently disagrees from that moment.

**⭐ It compares BEHAVIOUR, not spelling.** A pathspec and an ERE cannot be string-compared. Both are applied to **every tracked file** (`git ls-files` — a walk, not a curated list), and the pathspec verdict is obtained by **asking git itself** (`git ls-files -- . ':(exclude)…'`) rather than reimplementing glob semantics, so it cannot drift from what `git diff` actually does. ⭐ **Mutation-proven, 3 of 3, and the third is the one that would have made this vacuous: widening `vercel.json` alone reds it; widening `ci.yml` alone reds it; and a broken extractor returning `[]` — which makes both sides "agree" perfectly — is caught by the not-vacuous control**, which requires each side to be shown separating a known doc from a known `.ts`.

**🔵 AND #61's LEVER (a) IS NOW SIZED, over 1,308 first-parent commits in 14 days.** The short-circuit works (9 of 20 deployments in one evening read `CANCELED`, all pure-docs), but the exclusion set is narrow: **`+ .github/**` saves 11 builds (2.3 %) · `+ supabase/tests/**` 2 (0.4 %) · `+ supabase/migrations/**` 129 (26.7 %) · all three 144 (29.8 %) of 484.** ⭐ **~90 % of the saving is one path.** At this item's own shape (build compute = 75 % of a $412 cycle) that is on the order of **$80/cycle** — the largest un-shipped lever on #61. Three real examples in one evening, each a full production build for a change `next build` cannot see: a comment-only `.sql` migration edit, a comment-only workflow edit, a comment-only `vitest.config.ts` edit.

**🚨 THE RISK IS IN THE SAME PLACE AS THE PRIZE, so it is filed, not shipped.** `ignoreCommand` diffs `HEAD^..HEAD`, so excluding a path means a push whose TIP is that path does not deploy — and migrations ship *with* app code constantly. **Measured: 17 of 131 migration/test-only commits have a parent touching `app/`/`lib/`/`components/`/`workers/`** — 17 places where the app code would have merged green and never shipped. ⚠ Upper bound (the parent may have been pushed separately), but not zero. **Trevor's call: 2.7 % safe, or 26.7 % with "commit the migration BEFORE the code" as a standing order** — the same discipline already mandated for the ledger, now with a guard that reds if the two gates drift.

**Gates:** `npm test` **1515 files / 16,933 tests, all pass** · `tsc` clean · `lint:ratchet` at baseline · 3/3 mutations killed · `check-memory-doc-links` 196 · ledger guards 3 / 0.

### 2026-09-12 · ⭐ CODE+DB — the Cowork (g) standing order, items 2–4: one collector's whole trophy case was a blank slab, and `thumbnail_url` was the one display field the trophy RPC never resolved live

**Shipped:** `supabase/migrations/20260913040000_audit_20260913_trophy_art_falls_back_to_the_live_edition_render.sql` (APPLIED, live — RPC change **plus a one-row data repair**), `supabase/tests/get_trophy_slab_data.sql`, `__tests__/db-invariants-drift-guard.test.ts` (pin repointed), `lib/profile/trophy-thumbnail.ts`, `app/api/og/profile/[username]/route.tsx`, `app/api/og/trophy-case/[username]/route.tsx`, `__tests__/trophy-pin-does-not-publish-client-asserted-art-or-serial.test.ts`. Revert: header of the migration (it records the exact broken value being replaced) + `git revert` the commit whose message starts `fix(trophy): resolve art live`.

**⭐ ITEM 3, AND THE WRITER IS NAMED: `get_trophy_slab_data` PASSED `tm.thumbnail_url` STRAIGHT THROUGH.** Every other display field in that function is `COALESCE(e.<live>, tm.<snapshot>)` — player, set, tier, circulation, video, FMV, badges. Art sat in the middle of that column **with no live side at all**. So the malformed URL Cowork spotted on `blaise_27`'s card was never repaired by anything: `trophy_moments` stores `…/play_<uuid>_<set>_capture_/image` — a Top Shot static filename cut off at `capture_` with the render endpoint's `/image` glued on — while `editions.thumbnail_url` for the same edition (233:8334, Victor Wembanyama, Metallic Gold LE) is intact. ⚠ **And `lib/profile/trophy-thumbnail.ts` ALREADY SAID SO** ("two stored fields are NOT coalesced") while its own docstring promised a rejected pin means *"the art simply falls back"*. **It did not fall back. It rendered ART UNAVAILABLE.** A comment that names a gap is not a guard against it.

**⛔ THE OBVIOUS FIX WAS THE WRONG ONE, and the measurement is the whole reason.** Making art consistent with its neighbours — `COALESCE(e.thumbnail_url, tm.thumbnail_url)` — reads as tidying and is a regression: over the 22 live trophy rows, 13 store art identical to the edition's, 1 has no edition to resolve, and **8 differ — of which SEVEN store `assets.nbatopshot.com/media/<nft_id>/image?width=180|512`, a per-serial derivative of ~31 KB, against an `editions` master that is a 2880×2880 PNG of 4–7 MB** (several of them over the OG card's own 4 MB cap — the same population the earlier entry tonight is about). Live-first would have swapped eight working thumbnails for eight masters and called it a fix. Shipped as `COALESCE(tm.thumbnail_url, e.thumbnail_url)`: **a fallback, not a preference.** ⚠ **Zero rows change from the function alone** (no trophy row has a NULL thumbnail today) — what it buys is that `sanitizeTrophyThumbnail()` rejecting a URL now degrades to the edition's own art instead of to nothing, which is what makes the writer-side hardening in the same push safe rather than destructive.

**Writer hardened, and the rule I did NOT write is the point.** `sanitizeTrophyThumbnail` allowlisted the HOST and never looked at the SHAPE. "An `/editions/` path must end in an image extension" would have **rejected all 6,190 NFL All Day editions**, which address art as the perfectly valid extensionless `/editions/<n>/media/image`. The discriminator is the `play_` segment — that is what marks a STATIC FILENAME — and a static filename that is not the last path segment has been truncated. Three whole-population controls are pinned alongside it (intact TS static, All Day, TS's own `/media/<id>/image` render endpoint).

**⭐ ITEM 2 — `trophyGrid(1)` CAPTION GEOMETRY, and the live distribution is why it matters.** Everything on a trophy tile derives from `grid.w` — the slab, the art, the badge glyphs at `w/7` — except the serial/tier caption, hardcoded at 10px in a 15px band. On the six-slab case that is right; on the hero slab (240×317, nearly 4× the area) it is a sliver. ⚠ **And the hero is the COMMON case:** measured live, of the 7 collectors who have pinned anything, **4 have exactly one trophy and 3 have six — nobody in between**, which is exactly the "4 of 7" Cowork reported. Caption now scales as `clamp(10, 14, w/17)` with the height following; **floored at today's value so the six- and four-slab cases are byte-identical** (130/17 and 138/17 both round to 8, which the floor lifts back to 10).

**ITEM 4 — the Simba one-line clamp is a CSS clamp, not a budget retune.** The set/context lines sit in `height: 13, overflow: hidden` boxes and the character budget (`floor(w / 5.6)`) over-counts: at 10px mono with 0.3 letter-spacing a glyph advances ~6.3px, so ~12% more characters are allowed than fit, and the overrun **wrapped** — two ~12px lines centred in a 13px box means BOTH are sliced through the middle. Disney Pinnacle is where it shows because its set names are the long ones (` Walt Disney Animation Studios • The Lion King Vol.2`). Shipped `whiteSpace: "nowrap"`, which cannot over-clip. ⚠ **The divisor is deliberately NOT retuned: that 6.3 is arithmetic, not a measurement of the font satori actually loaded**, and tightening it on arithmetic would ellipsise text that fits today. Nothing in CI measures layout, so what a corrected budget would buy — the "…" landing in the right place — needs a rendered card.

**🚨 THE NEAR-MISS WORTH MORE THAN ANY OF IT: I ALMOST SILENTLY REVERTED ANOTHER SESSION'S GUARD.** I dumped `get_trophy_slab_data` at ~03:15Z, built the migration on it, and **re-read the live definition immediately before applying** — 3,077 characters had become **3,873**. `20260911093000` (the impossible-serial guard, "refuse a serial above its own edition's circulation") had landed in between. ### 2026-09-12 · ✅ CODE — #91's own instrument could never size #91: a bounded caller cannot measure the latency of the thing it bounds · Claude Code cloud, Trevor: "keep going"

**Shipped:** `app/api/badge-image/route.ts`, `__tests__/api-badge-image.test.ts` (+3), `docs/reference/known-issues.md` (#91). Revert: `git revert` the commit whose message starts `fix(badge-image): measure the upstream round trip`. **Logging only — no behaviour change, no DB, no schema.**

**⭐ THE FINDING, AND IT IS ABOUT AN INSTRUMENT RATHER THAN A LATENCY.** #91 ends by saying its new caller-side log *"carries elapsed-vs-budget, so option (a) can be sized from real data instead of feel — that is what it is for."* ⛔ **It cannot be.** `lib/og/official-mark-art.ts` truncates itself at `OFFICIAL_ART_BUDGET_MS = 4_000`, so its `elapsed` is **≈ the budget by construction** — and both observed instances prove it: **4007ms** and **4013ms**. The line records **THAT we gave up**, never **WHAT WE WOULD HAVE WAITED**, which is the only number option (a) ("raise to ~6–7s") can be sized from. ⭐ **A bounded caller cannot measure the latency of the thing it bounds** — and the callee logged nothing at all on the success path, which is exactly the cold-but-eventually-fine case that matters.

**What shipped:** `/api/badge-image` now times its own round trip across **fetch AND body read** (the caller's budget covers both; stopping at the headers would under-report precisely the slow case) and logs `elapsed_ms` above a **1,000 ms** threshold. ⚠ **Censored below that ON PURPOSE and it is not a distribution** — warm hits dominate and would bury the tail; the tail is the question.

**⚠ A SHADOWING BUG FOUND WHILE EDITING, worth more than it looks.** Both failure branches did `const name = err instanceof Error ? err.name : 'unknown'`, which **shadowed the badge slug read at the top of the handler**. So `name=` printed `TimeoutError` on a failure line and `rookieMint` on a success line — **one key, two meanings, depending on which branch emitted it**, and the failure line never said which badge failed. Now `name=` is the slug and `err=` the class, which is what lets a callee line be joined to the URLs the caller lists when it gives up.

**🔵 AND A FIRST SIZING DATUM FELL OUT OF THE LOGS — it points at ~6 s.** At the 01:59:18 occurrence the caller gave up after 4013 ms naming **6 distinct url(s)**, and **six `/api/badge-image` requests logged `cache=MISS` at 01:59:20** — same count, two seconds later. Vercel emits its request line on completion, so those trips began ≈01:59:14 and finished ≈01:59:20: **≈6 s cold**, i.e. a 4 s budget misses and 6–7 s would have caught them. ⚠ **ONE datum, 1-second granularity, resting on the completion-time assumption — suggestive, not a level.**

**⛔ THE BUDGET IS DELIBERATELY NOT RAISED.** #91's own instruction is *"DO NOT JUST RAISE THE NUMBER AGAIN — that is how this was wrong the first time (2.5s, sized by analogy)"*, and one inferred datum is not a sizing. **Exit recorded on the item:** read `elapsed_ms` off the new lines in a few days — p95 under ~6 s → raise to p95 + headroom; **nothing logged at all → the cold path is rarer than three observations suggest and option (c) is the answer.** Both outcomes are now decidable; neither was before.

**⚠ POPULATION CAVEAT I ALMOST OMITTED: all three occurrences in 24 h are `jamesdillonbond` cards** — Trevor's own profile, i.e. **testing traffic, not organic crawler traffic**. "3 in 24 h" must not be read as a user-impact rate, and this item's commercial argument rests on crawlers, which do not appear in the sample at all.

### 2026-09-12 · ⭐ CODE — the OG byte cap was stripping art from 100% of Ultimates and 0% of Commons; card art now goes through `/_next/image`

**Shipped:** `lib/og/img-data.ts` (new `ogOptimizedTarget()` + an `optimize` opt), `lib/og/official-mark-art.ts` (badge glyphs opt out), `__tests__/og-img-data.test.ts` (+13 cases, 48 total). No DB, no migration. Revert: `git revert` the commit whose message starts `fix(og): route oversized card art through the image optimizer`.

**⭐ THE DEFECT, AND THE CORRELATION IS THE WHOLE STORY.** `ogImageDataUri` caps art at 4 MB and drops anything larger to the grey placeholder. Dapper's artwork gets richer as the tier rises — foils, particles, transparency in a 2880×2880 PNG — so the cap behaves as a filter that removes art from **exactly the Moments people most want to share**. Cowork measured six random `/editions/` files per tier: **ULTIMATE 6/6 over the cap (median 6.73 MB) · LEGENDARY 5/6 · RARE 4/6 · FANDOM 4/6 · COMMON 0/6 (median 3.21 MB)**, and rendered the two ends — edition `220:8093` (Walter Clayton Jr., ULTIMATE, $1,350) published a **blank 36,440 B card**; `133:4738` (Marcus Smart, COMMON, $0.39) published full art at 167,677 B. Weighted against the population, ≈2,950 of 8,405 editions over the cap, **including all 206 Ultimates**. ⚠ n=6 per tier is indicative, not a census — the direction and the Ultimate result are what is solid.

**The fix is a URL wrapper on infrastructure already deployed:** art no origin will size for us is now fetched through our own `/_next/image?url=…&w=640&q=75` (already allowed to crawlers — `app/robots.ts` 09-06 — and already permitted for these hosts by `next.config.ts` `remotePatterns`). Cowork measured 119,162 B of PNG back for that 7,677,876 B Ultimate: **64× smaller**, three orders of magnitude under the cap. ⛔ **Raising `maxBytes` would have been the wrong fix** — at 7 MB the base64 data URI is ~9.3 MB, past the 7.67 MB satori failure the module already documents. The cap is correct; the payload was the defect.

**⭐ THE PART THAT WAS RE-DERIVED RATHER THAN TRUSTED, because the whole fix turns on the optimizer handing satori a format it can decode.** Read out of the INSTALLED Next 16.2.9, not from memory or from Cowork's single sample: `images.formats` defaults to `["image/webp"]`, and `getSupportedMimeType` negotiates a format **only when `accept.includes(it)`** (`image-optimizer.js:222`) — `image/*` does not contain the literal `image/webp`, so it converts nothing and a PNG upstream returns PNG (`:1118`). ⛔ **The existing `Accept: image/*` header is therefore load-bearing, not decorative** — naming webp or avif there would blank every card. Same source settles the two magic numbers: `qualities` defaults to `[75]` (anything else is a 400) and `w` must be in `deviceSizes ∪ imageSizes`, where **640 is the smallest entry still covering the largest slot any card draws** (the moment card's 550px pane). All three are pinned by importing `imageConfigDefault` into the test, so a Next bump that moves them reds the suite instead of silently 400ing back to blank cards.

**⚠ A `width=` PARAM IS NOT A TEST OF WHETHER ART IS SIZED, and getting that wrong would have re-opened this defect on the exact surface it was filed from.** Two origins genuinely pre-size their art (`assets.nbatopshot.com/media/<nft_id>/image?width=400` → 31,507 B; `media.nflallday.com/editions/<n>/media/image?width=512` → 45,121 B) and are skipped, because optimizing them buys nothing and would **UPSCALE** them — sharp enlarges by default. But `hiResThumb()` appends `?width=640` to **every** `assets.nbatopshot.com` url including the 2880×2880 statics, where the origin ignores it — so the test is a size param **on an extensionless render endpoint**, and a static image file is never "already sized" whatever query it carries. Both trophy cards run through `hiResThumb`.

**⛔ STRICTLY NO-WORSE BY CONSTRUCTION: the direct fetch is always the fallback.** One shared 4.5s budget across both legs (a dead upstream must not cost 9s because we asked two ways), and an optimizer refusal — a `remotePatterns` drift, an input sharp won't touch, or the `next start` / Vercel difference on a LOCAL url that answers 302 (the Pinnacle resolver does) — lands on exactly today's behaviour. **The optimizer leg can add art, never remove it.** Pinned with a positive case AND a no-change control (`optimize:false` on the same oversized art still yields the blank card), so the headline case is measuring the optimizer rather than a mock that would pass either way. Both magic numbers were mutation-checked: `q=80` and `w=384` each red the suite.

**⚠ THE FILED DECISION NOT TO ACT THAT THIS OVERTURNS, AND IT OVERTURNS ONLY HALF OF IT.** The 2026-08-2x HeroMontage entry rejected `/_next/image` outright: *"Vercel bills image optimization per source image transformed, so with ~19.5k TS editions routing it through `/_next/image` would create a real metered bill."* That was right for **HTML page tiles** — five montage tiles on every page view, at several widths — and this is a different population: **OG cards only, one width, one quality**, and the two pre-sized origins (9,416 rows) are skipped entirely. Worst case is **≈14.3k unique `(source, w=640, q=75)` transformations** — TS statics 8,405 + Golazos 575 + IPFS proxy 2,886 + Pinnacle ≤2,412 — and only for editions a crawler actually fetches inside one cache window. 🚨 **STATED AS A UNIT COUNT, NOT A PRICE: the sandbox has no Vercel egress, so the per-transformation rate and the Pro allowance were NOT re-measured tonight. Trevor should eyeball Usage → Image Optimization once before this is called free.** The zero-cost alternative if it ever matters is known and unbuilt: Top Shot's own CDN resizes `media/<rep_nft_id>/image?width=N` (1,460× on the 08-2x measurement), but the OG routes carry `thumbnail_url`, not a rep nft id, so that is an RPC change across several routes rather than a URL wrapper. The off-switch here is one word — `optimize: false`.

**⚠ A RED I FOUND, DID NOT TOUCH, AND WATCHED SOMEONE ELSE FIX MID-SESSION.** `npm test` was RED on `main` at `91980fe29` — `migration-new-function-states-its-anon-exec-decision` on `20260913021000_audit_…at_open_basis.sql → public.backfill_pack_rip_metadata`, reproduced on a clean stash of that tree, so not this work's. Left alone deliberately: another session's in-flight migration, and re-splicing someone else's file mid-flight is how collisions happen. **That call was right — `c5428d41c` ("state the anon-exec decision the realign migration dropped") landed upstream while this was being built, and the guard is green on the rebased tree.** ⚠ Recorded because the finding and its fix are ~40 minutes apart and the entry would otherwise read as a still-open red. **Gates on the rebased tree: `tsc --noEmit` clean · `lint:ratchet` 715/716 · the six `check-*` guards 0 · full coverage run 92.13 / 80.23 / 94.3 / 94.2 against thresholds 91.8 / 79.4 / 93.6 / 93.85, with `img-data.ts` at 97.4% statements.**

### 2026-09-12 · ✅ CODE — the official-art budget was measured wrong and the memo cached the miss; production found both within the hour · Cowork cloud, follow-up to the 09-12(d) badge-art ship

**Shipped:** `lib/og/official-mark-art.ts` (budget 2.5s → 4s, failures no longer memoized, the warning now carries elapsed ms + the failing URLs) and one new case in `__tests__/og-cards-use-official-badge-art.test.ts`. Revert: `git revert` the commit whose message starts `fix(og): official badge art gave up before the proxy answered`.

**⭐ THE INSTRUMENT FOUND ITS OWN AUTHOR'S MISTAKE, WHICH IS THE ONLY REASON THIS IS A ONE-HOUR BUG.** The warning line added yesterday — *"official art unavailable for N mark(s); RPC glyphs drawn instead"* — fired on the FIRST live render of the trophy-case card after deploy. Without it the card looks perfect: an RPC glyph is a good-looking badge, so a card that silently stopped drawing official art is visually identical to one that never tried.

**The measurement, production, 2026-09-13.** Rendered `/api/og/trophy-case/jamesdillonbond` live and read the logs for the same request: **all 6 `/api/badge-image` requests returned 200 with `cache=MISS`, and 4 of the 6 marks still fell back.** The proxy served every one; the client gave up first. Nothing was broken — the budget was simply shorter than a cold CDN round trip.

**⚠ DEFECT 1 — A BUDGET SIZED BY ANALOGY TO THE WRONG THING.** 2.5s was picked to match the jersey-number read, "the other read on this path whose failure costs a glyph". But that is a read of OUR OWN DATABASE. This one waits on `/api/badge-image`, a PROXY that on an edge-cache MISS must itself fetch Dapper's CDN — and **that route bounds its own upstream at `UPSTREAM_TIMEOUT_MS = 8_000`**. ⭐ **A client budget below the bound of the thing it is waiting on can only ever truncate a request the proxy would have served.** Now 4s (matching `server-art.ts`'s `BADGE_ART_TIMEOUT_MS`, the repo's existing sized precedent) — and because the fetches run CONCURRENTLY in one `Promise.all`, that bounds the whole PASS, not each URL: worst case 4s once, not 4s per badge.

**🚨 DEFECT 2 — THE MEMO CACHED THE MISS, AND THAT IS UNBOUNDED IN THE WRONG DIRECTION.** It was documented as deliberate ("one attempt per instance, not one per card"). It is wrong here and wrong in the way that hides itself: `/api/badge-image` is edge-cached **24h** (`max-age=86400, stale-while-revalidate=604800`), so a failure is almost always a COLD-CACHE failure — **and the act of failing WARMS it**. The retry a cached miss forbids is precisely the one that would have succeeded, instantly. Cost of being wrong: ONE slow cold start poisons every card that lambda serves for the rest of its life, drawing RPC glyphs on every share while the asset sits warm at the edge. Successes are still cached for the instance's life (the asset is immutable) and the in-flight promise is still shared, which is what the dedupe actually needs; only the miss is dropped.

**⚠ THE GENERAL LESSON, worth more than either fix: A TIMEOUT IS A CLAIM ABOUT WHAT YOU ARE WAITING ON, NOT ABOUT WHAT YOU CAN AFFORD.** Both defects came from reasoning about the CALLER's comfort (a decoration should not cost much) with no model of the CALLEE's cost. The repo already had the number — it is a named constant in the route being called. **Read the callee's own bound before choosing yours**, and when the callee is cached, ask what the FIRST caller pays versus the second.

**⚠ And a negative result is not a fact about the world — it is a fact about one attempt at one moment.** Caching it is caching a measurement, which CLAUDE.md's "a figure is a DATED SAMPLE" rule already says not to do; this is that rule showing up in control flow rather than in prose.

**The warning now carries the numbers.** `after {elapsed}ms (budget {N}ms, {k} distinct url(s))` plus the failing URLs — because "unavailable for 4 mark(s)" said something was wrong and nothing about why, and cost a round trip to diagnose. Elapsed-against-budget IS the diagnosis: at the budget means truncated by us, far under it means the proxy said no. The next misjudgement should be findable without a redeploy.

**Verified:** `npx tsc --noEmit` clean · the 6 affected suites 125 pass / 0 fail · new case pins BOTH directions (a cold failure retries and succeeds; the success is then cached and does not re-fetch).

**⚠ Still unverified and stated as such:** whether 4s is ENOUGH for a cold MISS. It is 60% more than the number production just refuted and matches a sized precedent, but the cold latency of `/api/badge-image` was never measured directly — that is what the new log fields exist to answer on the next cold render. The self-healing retry is the belt to that braces: even if 4s is short, the second render of any card in that PoP now gets official art.

### 2026-09-12 · ✅ CODE — I reddened `main`: the TS-oracle's non-vacuity control walked the tree twice and timed out on CI · Claude Code cloud, self-inflicted

**Shipped:** `__tests__/strip-comments-matches-typescript.test.ts`. Revert: `git revert` the commit whose message starts `fix(tests): the TS-oracle's non-vacuity control walked the tree twice`.

**What happened.** The oracle shipped an hour earlier (register #87) carried a control — *"the comparison is not simply reporting zero for everything"* — that re-parsed all **3,008 files** with the TypeScript compiler **inside an `it()`**, to re-derive a number the sweep above had already computed. **7.4 s on this 16-core idle box; over the 30 s `testTimeout` on a 2-core CI runner under coverage instrumentation.** CI shard 1/2 failed; 17 of 18 jobs were green and shard 2/2 finished in 2m40s against shard 1's 309 s.

⭐ **THE FULL SUITE HAD JUST PASSED LOCALLY, AND THAT READING WAS WORTH NOTHING.** *A probe whose HARNESS differs from production in the one dimension the answer depends on is not a measurement of production* — the dimension here was CPU count and coverage instrumentation, and "it passed on my box" is exactly that probe. The repo's own rule, applied to a test rather than to a fetch.

**Fix:** the count comes off the single sweep that already parses every file; the two positive controls drop 400 → 150 files. TypeScript parsing now happens **exactly once** in this file. Worst test under coverage **7.4 s → 1.47 s**, file test time **11 s → 2.9 s**. ⚠ The expensive sweep **stays at describe scope deliberately** — collection is not bounded by `testTimeout`, and moving it to a `beforeAll` would bound it by the **30 s `hookTimeout`**, which is the same trap one level over.

⚠ **A SECOND LESSON, about the instrument I used to check my own work.** `get_job_logs(failed_only: true)` returned **"No failed jobs found, 18 total"** while shard 1/2 had ALREADY failed at 00:44 — the run list still showed it `in_progress`. **A "no failures" reading on a run that has not concluded is not evidence of green**, and it reads identically to success. Read the JOB's log, not the run's summary, and check the job's own `completed_at`.

**Gates:** `npm test` **1510 files / 16,842 tests, all pass**; the oracle re-verified under `--coverage`, the way CI runs it, not bare.

### 2026-09-12 · ✅ CODE — the shared comment stripper was blind on 10 files and DESTROYING source on 2; it is now JSX-aware and pinned against the TypeScript compiler · Claude Code cloud, Trevor: "testing and CI improvements"

**Shipped:** `scripts/lib/strip-comments.mjs` (JSX awareness + a fifth, unrelated defect), `__tests__/strip-comments-matches-typescript.test.ts` (NEW — the oracle), `__tests__/strip-comments-defect-4-population.test.ts` (both ratchets → bans at zero), `__tests__/strip-comments-shared-helper.test.ts` (DEFECT 4 pins INVERTED, not deleted), `__tests__/helpers/source-files.ts` (the shared tree walk), plus `CLAUDE.md`, `docs/reference/testing-and-ci.md`, `docs/reference/known-issues.md` (#87 → closed). Revert: `git revert` the commit whose message starts `fix(guards): make the shared comment stripper JSX-aware`.

**What was wrong.** Register **#87**: a JS/TS parser run over `.tsx`, where an apostrophe in JSX prose opened an `sq` state that copied everything verbatim — comments included — and handed them to every guard in the repo as source. Measured at the start of this session: **10 files, 899 lines**. Fixed at the root with two states, `jsxTag` (quotes ARE attribute delimiters, `{` opens an expression container) and `jsxText` (quotes, `//` and `/* */` are all prose), sharing one stack with `${…}` so `{cond && <b>x</b>}` nests and `{/* … */}` needs no special case. **Census 10 / 899 → 0 / 0.**

**⭐⭐ THE DELIVERABLE IS THE ORACLE, NOT THE FIX.** `strip-comments-matches-typescript.test.ts` parses every file with the TypeScript compiler and asserts its comment ranges are EXACTLY what the stripper blanks — both directions, two bans at zero, **3,008 / 3,008 files agreeing**. All five defects in this file were found by accident months late and then pinned by a fixture describing the case just found; **a fixture can only assert the defect its author already knows about**, and the contract was never a list of cases. Mutation-proven: disabling the JSX branch reds both directions with file and line.

**🚨 IT REFUTED THE DEFECT'S OWN SAFETY CLAIM.** The header and the register both said DEFECT 4 *"fails in the SAFE direction … never blanks code"*. **False — 2 files, 46 characters of real source BLANKED**, DEFECT 3's direction, the one that hid a live P0. JSX text was never a string state; it was parsed as CODE, so `//` in a URL opened a line comment. `app/(analytics)/analytics/api/page.tsx:116` gave every guard `"            https:                      "` where the production base URL is printed on a public page. ⭐ **Why it stood 16 days: the census counted the `sq`/`dq` SYMPTOM, which really is safe — so an instrument built on it reports the safe half completely, and the unsafe half of the same root cause is invisible to it by construction.** Never derive a claim about a DEFECT from an instrument that measures one of its SYMPTOMS.

**⭐ A FIFTH DEFECT, unrelated to JSX.** `word` accumulated identifier characters across whitespace — `continue` on one line and `return` on the next made `continuereturn`, not a keyword, so the regex after it read as DIVISION. An identical regex desynced or not depending only on what sat on the previous line. It had desynced `__tests__/helpers-client-directive.test.ts` for months, attributed to nothing, because its symptom (`dq`) looks exactly like DEFECT 4's.

**⛔ THREE THINGS I GOT WRONG, each caught by an instrument rather than by review.** (1) My first two oracles were wrong before the stripper was, reporting 2,945 then 905 confident false findings with real file names — a char mask cannot see blanking of characters that were already spaces, and a comment on the same line as the preceding token is TRAILING trivia that `getLeadingCommentRanges` excludes by design. (2) I sized the residual `<`-ambiguity by grepping `<tag>(`, wrote "zero instances" into the header, and the census then failed on `<> (last updated {d})</>` — a FRAGMENT the pattern could not match. **A guard's population must be counted by the guard's own predicate, not by a regex that resembles it.** (3) The oracle imported `walk` from the census *test* file, which re-registered that whole suite — it ran twice, attributed to the wrong filename; caught by counting tests per file, not by any failure.

**Gates:** re-run AFTER rebasing onto six concurrent commits, because a reading taken while its subject changed is not a reading — census and oracle both re-measured on the merged tree (**3,008 / 3,008**, 0 / 0). `npm test` **1510 files / 16,842 tests, all pass**; this session's own net is **+18** (30 tests added, **−12** for the duplicated census suite it removed) against the 16,803 baseline, the rest being upstream's. ### 2026-09-12 · ✅ CODE — the nav's active tab was signalled by COLOUR ALONE, and the one active tab announced `aria-pressed="false"` · Cowork cloud, production verification of the re-slot

**Shipped:** `components/MobileNav.tsx` (`aria-current` on the active tab) and `__tests__/component-MobileNav.test.tsx` (+4 tests, and an annotation on the focus test that matters more than the fix). Revert: `git revert` the commit whose message starts `fix(nav): announce the active tab, not just colour it`.

**Found by walking the re-slot in production**, not by reading the diff. On `/nba-top-shot/overview` the COLLECTIONS tab rendered in the active red while carrying **`aria-pressed="false"` and no `aria-current`** — so the one tab that WAS the answer told a screen reader it was not pressed, and **no tab anywhere exposed "you are here" at all**. Colour was the entire active signal, which is also the signal that fails for anyone who cannot separate `#e03a2f` from 55% white. Read from the live DOM on the deploy, all five tabs, `aria-current: null` on every one.

**⚠ THE TWO ATTRIBUTES ANSWER DIFFERENT QUESTIONS, and COLLECTIONS needs both.** `aria-pressed` is about the **sheet** (it is a disclosure control); `aria-current` is about the **location**. On a collection page with the sheet closed they correctly disagree — `aria-current="page"` and `aria-pressed="false"` — and a test now pins exactly that pair, because the tempting "fix" is to make `aria-pressed` track the route, which would then lie about whether the sheet is open. SEARCH is a pure disclosure and never claims a location.

**⭐⭐ THE FINDING THAT MATTERS MORE THAN THE FIX: AN OCCLUDED CHROME WINDOW MAKES EVERY rAF BEHAVIOUR READ AS BROKEN.** While verifying the new Search sheet I measured that focus never entered it — **zero `focusin` events across a close and a reopen**, on the Collections sheet too, which has shipped for weeks. The obvious conclusion was that `useModalA11y`'s focus trap does not work in a real browser and the jsdom test only passes because it **mocks `requestAnimationFrame` to fire synchronously**. That conclusion was WRONG, and one probe away from being filed as a defect: the Chrome window was **occluded behind File Explorer**, `document.visibilityState === "hidden"`, and **a probe `requestAnimationFrame` never fired in 1500 ms**. Chrome suspends rAF entirely in a hidden tab.

⚠ **So the browser harness used for this project's UI verification cannot measure anything deferred to a frame** — focus traps, transitions, animations, lazy mounts, IntersectionObserver work — and each will present as a confident, reproducible, *false* defect. Recorded at the focus test itself, where the next person to doubt it will be standing. **Raise the window first, or the finding is about the harness and not the product.**

**What DID verify in production** on `b0c7762`: exactly **one** nav bar on `/dashboard/packs` (no double mount) · labels 🏠HOME 🔍SEARCH ⚡SNIPER 👤MY STUFF 🗂COLLECTIONS · hrefs `/`, `/nba-top-shot/sniper`, **`/profile`** — the login wall stays closed · **`/nba-top-shot/overview` lights COLLECTIONS** (`rgb(224,58,47)` against `rgba(255,255,255,0.55)`), the gap that used to light nothing · `/insights/candy-mlb` has a bar at all · the Search sheet opens with its input, and opening it closes the Collections sheet.

This one catches a pipeline that **succeeds, writes rows, and still loses**: `reconcile-saved-wallet-stats` sweeps a bounded batch under a soft deadline and **commits the partial result**, so it is working-as-designed on every single run while the backlog behind it grows without limit.

**Measured 2026-09-12: all three existing instruments read healthy straight through a 16-hour drain.** Pipeline Silence — the cron fired every hour, exactly on time. `detect_stalled_pipelines()` — keys on recency; the runs were recent. Pipeline Success Coverage — its predicate is *zero successes AND zero rows written*, and ⭐ **this pipeline is the NAMED REASON that `AND` exists**: it was 2 of the 4 false positives the `rows_written` guard was added to remove. So the one arm that could have fired is deliberately, correctly blind here. ⛔ **Do not "fix" that by loosening the guard** — it would restore 4 known false positives to catch one thing. Asking the outcome question instead is the cheaper trade.

**⭐ THE METRIC IS THE PIPELINE'S OWN, and that is the whole point.** Every run already writes `extra.oldest_cache_h`. That is not a proxy for the user-visible quantity, it **IS** the user-visible quantity — the dashboard's new "as of Nh ago" caption reads from the very same `saved_wallets.cached_*` columns. The arm reads the caption the product is printing.

**Thresholds are CONTRACT-DERIVED, then checked against history — not fitted to it.** The cron fires hourly and only considers rows older than `min_age_minutes` (360), so the design guarantee is ~6h plus one sweep; **warn at 12h** means a full cycle was missed. Replayed over all **79 runs in retention** (09-09 → 09-12): the **74 runs during the known drain** hit p50 **7.0h** / max **17.0h** and would have warned **14 times**; the **5 runs after it** hit p50 **0.9h** / max **6.2h** and would have warned **zero** times. ⚠ **The quiet side is only 5 runs — thin, and the comment says so.** ⚠ **Crit (24h) has NEVER fired**, including through that drain, and is **not calibrated**: it sits deliberately above the worst thing ever observed, so it means "the drain is losing to the inflow", not "the drain is deep".

**⭐ THE READING AGES TOO, and that term is the arm's novel half.** `oldest_cache_h` was true when its run took it and **can only have gotten worse since**, so the arm reports `oldest_cache_h + (now − started_at)` and labels it a **lower bound** (`>=19.0h`). A 5h cache measured 14h ago is a 19h cache. This is also what keeps the arm honest if the cron stops, without it becoming a second cadence check. ⚠ **A status-only test on a FRESH reading passes just as happily with this term deleted** — verified by mutation: removing `+ readingAgeH` fails exactly 2 of the 8 new tests, and they are the two written for it.

**⚠ UNREADABLE IS NOT ZERO.** A run that publishes no `extra.oldest_cache_h` reads **warn / "the cache depth is UNREADABLE, not zero"** with `value` **omitted rather than zeroed** — otherwise a future reconcile that stopped emitting the key would park this arm at "ok" forever, which is a failed read rendering as an answer. An **empty `pipeline_runs` window is CRITICAL**, same reasoning as Ownership: retention is ~73h, so the query goes empty exactly when the outage has outlived it. Saturation → warn, never a page.

**⚠ THE TEST FIXTURE IS NOW A SEQUENCE, and that is load-bearing.** Three arms read `pipeline_runs` in order (Ownership → this → notification delivery). The harness hands successive calls successive array elements; a single object would have fed all three the same payload and this arm would have correctly reported UNREADABLE, turning the green battery amber. Documented at the fixture.

**Gates:** `tsc` clean · **146 tests across all four sentinel suites** · eslint ratchet **716 vs baseline 716** · ledger guards 3 / 0. ⚠ Not yet verified in production — the hourly `pipeline-sentinel.yml` job echoes the response body in its GHA logs, which is the free verification path (no token, no `workflow_dispatch`, no page).

That is the Small-compute IO budget; another index only adds write amplification. **Do not add one.**

**What it serves instead.** `saved_wallets.cached_*`, written hourly by `aggregate_saved_wallet_stats` at ~335 ms — numbers that were correct the entire time the dashboard rendered `$0` (cached counts matched `wallet_moments_cache` to within ~0.1%). The live RPC remains the fallback for a wallet with no cached row yet; those are small by definition. A cache read that FAILS or THROWS degrades to live rather than failing the request — both pinned.

**⚠ `covered_collection_ids` is the load-bearing part, and the entry above is why.** A cached read only covers collections the wallet has a row for, and **a missing row is not a zero** — six wallets had no UFC row while three held 247, 61 and 18 Moments. Zero-filling would have published "0 Moments" about a $1,547 holding: the same false-zero class, arriving through a new door. The card renders an uncovered collection as unknown. A payload with no `covered_collection_ids` (an older cached response) keeps the previous behaviour rather than blanking every tile — pinned as its own control.

### 2026-09-12 · ✅ SHIPPED: a backfiller reported **96 % success** for **2.8 % progress** — `dist_resolved` counted the rows that already had one · Claude Code (cloud), autonomous session

**Found while re-deriving #72, not from a filing.** `pipeline_runs.extra.dist_resolved` for `backfill-pack-rip-metadata` read **484 / 484 / 488 of 500** on three consecutive runs. ⭐ **The tell is not the size of the number, it is that the three barely move** — a drain working through a backlog reports a figure that falls as the backlog does.

🚨 **THE MECHANISM, and it is a one-word reading error with a 34× consequence.** The value came from `RETURNING pr.dist_id IS NOT NULL AS dist_resolved` over an `UPDATE … SET dist_id = COALESCE(bd.dist_id, pr.dist_id)`. **`RETURNING` yields the NEW row**, and `COALESCE` preserves whatever was already there — so the flag is true for **every row that ENDS UP with a dist_id, including every row that walked in with one.** The function's own candidate selection guarantees most did: its `stale_valued` arm takes 40 % of each batch from rows already processed once (`metadata_updated_at < now() - 7 days`), i.e. precisely the rows most likely to be resolved already. **The field measured the batch's composition, not the drain's progress.**

🚨 **THE PROBLEM, and it is structural rather than an oversight.** `rpc_trust_health_precompute` has **PRIMARY KEY (metric)** — one row per metric, overwritten every leg. **It cannot produce a series.** Every historical reading in go-live-2026-09.md was captured by hand by whoever happened to be looking at that leg. ⛔ **So the doc's own rule — *"no single leg is a level for M2 while the sweep is mid-cycle"*, *"quote a full-sweep reading or a matched comparison, never a leg"* — was UNFOLLOWABLE against the table it points at.** M2 swung **22.59 → 24.07 → 28.3 → 23.0 inside nine hours**, the 28.3 was written up as a +4.9-point gain and then retracted, and M1's *"two consecutive readings below 50"* trigger was evaluated from two hand-noted numbers. **A reader arriving later has one number and no way to tell where in the sweep it was taken.**

⭐ **PK (metric, computed_at) is the design, not bookkeeping:** it makes capture idempotent, so the job may run far faster than the legs and every repeat is free. The cadence then only has to beat the FASTEST metric's refresh rather than match the legs — and there is no de-duplication logic to get wrong.

**Today's leg, now the first row of that series (2026-09-12 07:48Z):** **M1 Top Shot `topshot_fmv_high_med_share_pct` = 56.3** (bar ≥50; sweep 80.0, fresh24h 70.3, stale_30d 0.0) · **M2 All Day = 29.9** (bar ≥30; sweep 55.4, fresh24h 53.8, stale_30d 0.0). ⛔ **NEITHER IS RECORDED AS A LEVEL, and M2 at 29.9 is one tenth of a point from the bar — which is exactly the reading most likely to be quoted wrongly.** Sweep is mid-cycle at 55.4 %, so by the doc's own rule this is a leg. **The point of this change is that the next reader will be able to tell.**

Security mirrors the precompute exactly (RLS true, anon false, authenticated false, service_role true). ⭐ **Idempotence measured, not argued: a repeat capture inserted 0 rows.** ⭐ **And a POSITIVE control, because an idempotence test alone would also pass for a capture that writes nothing:** a synthetic new `(metric, computed_at)` did land, and was cleaned up (0 `zz_%` rows remain). ⚠ **That control misled me first and it is recorded in the migration:** I wrote insert / verify / delete as three CTEs of ONE statement, and **CTEs in one statement do not see each other's writes** — so it reported "not visible, nothing deleted" while the row had been inserted and left behind. It took a second statement to clean up. **A self-cleaning probe needs separate statements, or it is neither.**

**Revert path.** `SELECT cron.unschedule('rpc-trust-health-history'); DROP TABLE public.rpc_trust_health_history;` — nothing else reads either, so no code revert is required.

### 2026-09-11 · ✅ SHIPPED: the HIGH-severity alarm that had been crying wolf for days was a real query defect — `fmv_backfill_candidates` now drives from `editions` (21,423 rows) instead of `sales` (4.9 M), 5.7× fewer buffers and no temp spill · Claude Code (cloud), autonomous session

**Shipped: migration `20260912063341`, its DB-invariant pin updated (fixture + verbatim DDL + a new assertion), `PINS` repointed. Applied in a measured quiet window.**

Found by taking an alert at face value and then testing the excuse attached to it. `rpc_ops_snapshot()` carried `fmv-backfill` at **8/12 runs failed (66.7 %), HIGH severity**, and the day's monitor filings had (reasonably) written it off as **spell collateral**. ⭐ **The spell had cleared, so the excuse was testable — and it half-held:** the lane's successes all land at quiet hours (23:24 · 01:23 · 06:11Z) and every failure at a busy one. **But every success reads `rows_found = 0, rows_written = 0`.** The attribution was right about the timeouts and silent about the more interesting fact: **when the lane works, it does nothing.**

🚨 **THE SHAPE IS THIS ESTATE'S LIMIT-NEVER-BINDS PATHOLOGY, and the plan says so exactly.** The old body scanned `sales` with `NOT EXISTS (fmv_snapshots)`, `GROUP BY`, `LIMIT 100` — a **Parallel Hash Anti Join over ALL EIGHT partitions** (2,446,494 rows × 2 workers) hashed against **743,191** snapshot rows, with the `LIMIT` sitting **above a Sort/Group where it cannot short-circuit**. With a true answer of **zero** the limit never binds, so every tick pays the entire scan. Its own `SET statement_timeout = '60s'` then decides the outcome by instance load.

⭐ **A/B ON ONE IDLE INSTANCE, warm-vs-warm so the comparison is not a cache artifact:**

```
BEFORE  427,727 buffers + 55,406 TEMP blocks (16 hash batches, spilled)  11,129 ms
AFTER    75,105 buffers, no temp                     3,237 ms cold / ~149 ms warm
```

### 2026-09-11 · 🧪 `npm test` IS GREEN ON THIS BOX AGAIN — a new guard's mutation cases were Windows-broken, and the overstatement I nearly shipped is the more useful half · Claude Code on Trevor's box, Trevor: "Keep going and doing anything you can"

**Shipped: `scripts/check-lane-egress.mjs` — the import walker now emits POSIX-separated paths. No test was changed, no classification moved. Full suite 1502 files / 16,671 tests, exit 0.**

⭐ **FOUND AS A BY-PRODUCT OF A CONTROL, NOT BY LOOKING FOR IT.** The full suite came back `2 failed` while I was verifying an unrelated pin fix. Rather than assume it was mine, I **stashed my work and re-ran on a clean tree — it failed identically**, which is the only thing that makes "not mine" a measurement instead of a hope.

**The mechanism.** `resolveSpec` used `path.resolve(path.dirname(fromFile), spec)`. On Windows that is platform-dependent twice: it emits `\` separators, **and given a rootless-POSIX base like `/r` it prepends the current DRIVE** — `path.resolve("/r", "./lib/remote")` → `C:\r\lib\remote`. The guard's `exists` is INJECTED (so its mutation cases can run against an in-memory tree, which is good design), and that tree is keyed `/r/lib/remote.ts`. The lookup missed, the import was never followed, and a lane with a fetch one level down classified `pure-db`. Fixed with a hand-rolled join that preserves a leading `/` and treats a `C:` drive as an ordinary segment, so real Windows roots and POSIX fixtures both round-trip.

🚨 **THE PART WORTH KEEPING IS THE CLAIM I WROTE FIRST AND THEN DISPROVED.** I wrote in the code comment that this was *"the guard failing OPEN — the exact direction it must never fail"*. **That is wrong, and one control killed it:** on a real tree the base is already an absolute Windows path, so `path.resolve` behaves. I checked out the **pre-fix** script and ran it — **same 11 lanes, same 2 pure-db, same evidence lines**; the only difference was `lib\chains\flow\topshot.ts:47` vs `lib/chains/…`, cosmetic. ⭐ **The guard was always correct in production on both platforms. What broke was its own mutation tests, and they broke LOUDLY — 2 of 18 red here, green on CI.** I corrected the comment before committing. **A plausible mechanism is not a measurement, even when the mechanism is real and the fix is right** — the mechanism was real, the blast radius I inferred from it was not.

⚠ **THE COST IS STILL REAL, WHICH IS WHY THIS WAS WORTH FIXING RATHER THAN ANNOTATING.** `npm test` could not be run green on the box where changes are verified by hand — and memory carries the invariant *"npm test is GREEN on this box — a red file MEANS something"*. **A permanently-red file trains a reader to ignore it**, which is precisely how a true red gets waved through; this repo has already paid for that with a permanently-red stall arm.

- 230 invocations / 72h, p50 **1,427 ms**, p95 **32,310 ms**, max **97,023 ms** (production-caller figures from the route's own `extra.duration_ms` — no probe fired, so no real user alerts were sent to measure it).

- Population: `alert_subscriptions` = **2 rows, 1 owner**. `alert_deliveries` = 3 in 30 days, 0 pending, 0 failed.

The June 834 came from a **different subscription that has since been deleted**; the two live subs were created 07-12 and 08-16. Positive control against the live boards (196 rows on `cross_collection_deals_board`, 29 on `topshot_underpriced_serials_board` — so neither board is empty): the Blazers sub matches **1** serial row, which is under its own 25% bar; the Lillard/Archive/≤$0.60 sub matches **0** on either board. **So the shipped artifact is the audit made permanent** — `scripts/check-lane-egress.mjs` + `npm run lanes:egress:check`, wired into `ci.yml`, 18 mutation tests.

🚨 **THE OBVIOUS CHECK IS WRONG, AND I RAN THE WRONG ONE FIRST.** `grep -cE 'fetch\(|https?://' <route>` returns **0 for four of the ten lanes** and is wrong on two: `snapshot-pack-asks` reaches Top Shot's GraphQL through `lib/packs/live-pack-listings.ts:233`, and `ownership-onchain-walk` reaches Flow through `@onflow/fcl`, which opens its own sockets with no visible `fetch` anywhere in this repo. ### 2026-09-10 · ⚠ A CAVEAT AGAINST MY OWN SHIP FROM MINUTES EARLIER: I put the new backstop INSIDE the documented lock-collision window, because I checked cron MINUTES and the thing that matters is how long the other job RUNS · Claude Code (cloud), Trevor: "Keep going"

**Shipped: `rpc-wmc-fmv-populate-backstop` rescheduled `3,18,33,48` → `4,24,44` (migration `20260911052600`). Function unchanged.**

🚨 **THE ERROR.** I chose `3,18,33,48` and justified it in the migration header: those minutes collide with neither jobid 302 (minutes ≡ 2 mod 5) nor jobid 303 (`7-57/10`). **That is true of the FIRING INSTANTS and irrelevant.** `app/api/wmc-fmv-populate/route.ts` records the actual behaviour: *"pg_cron jobid 303 runs a median of 240s, so the route's tick one minute later used to block ~18s on `wallet_moments_cache` row locks and die. **83 of 84 lock timeouts in 48h landed on :08/:18/:28/:38/:48/:58**, one minute after each 303 firing."* ⛔ **`:18` and `:48` are two of those exact minutes.** I had put a new job in the one window this repo has already measured as hostile.

⚠ **THE GENERAL LESSON, and it is the reason this is its own entry: a cron-collision check on MINUTES is a check on START TIMES. A job with a 4-minute median OCCUPIES four minutes of them.** 303 is busy 7–11, 17–21, 27–31, 37–41, 47–51, 57–01. **Ask what the other job's DURATION is, not only when it starts.**

**Shipped: `lib/telegram-message.ts` (new), wired into all three Telegram senders — `app/api/sentinel/route.ts`, `lib/ops-alert.ts`, `lib/allow-list/prewarm.ts` — plus `__tests__/telegram-alerts-are-bounded.test.ts` (11 cases). 🚨 **FOUND BY RUNNING THE THING, NOT BY READING IT.** I dispatched `Pipeline Sentinel` to verify the heartbeat change end-to-end, and the row it wrote carried this: `notifications: ["telegram-FAILED:http_400: {\"ok\":false,\"error_code\":400,\"description\":\"Bad Request: message is too long\"}", "email-FAILED:not_configured", "github-actions-native"]` on a **`status: CRITICAL`** sweep. ⭐ **Both out-of-band channels failed on the same run** — the alarm detected a real condition and the only surviving signal was a GitHub annotation.

⭐ **THE DEFECT IS THE SHAPE, AND IT IS THE WORST VERSION OF IT: the message is one line per check, and `Pipeline Silence` NAMES EVERY SILENT LANE.** So the message length is a function of how bad the incident is, and Telegram's `sendMessage` caps `text` at **4096 characters** and **REJECTS past it rather than truncating**. 🚨 **The alarm's delivery probability therefore FALLS AS THE THING IT REPORTS GETS WORSE** — it is least likely to arrive on exactly the runs that matter most, and its failure is visible only as silence. That is this estate's alert sub-class in its purest form.

✅ **FIXED AS A CLASS, NOT AT THE SITE.** A grep for the expression rather than the file found **three** unbounded senders (sentinel, `ops-alert`, allow-list `prewarm`), and the bound is applied **inside each sender**, not at the call site — a call site can always be copied without its length handling, which is how this repo has recorded this class spreading five times; a sender cannot be bypassed.

⭐ **THE CONTRACT IS NOT "IT FITS" — it is "it fits AND the reader can tell what was removed."** Lines are dropped in **severity order** (ok, then warn, then critical) but **rendered in original order**; the notice states how many of how many were dropped **and, when a critical had to go, NAMES it** — a bare count would let a reader conclude they had seen every critical. A single runaway detail is capped with its own visible marker instead of taking the other seventeen checks down with it, because a check's NAME and STATUS are worth more than its prose. ⛔ **Deliberately NOT split into multiple messages:** partial delivery (message 1 lands, message 2 400s) reintroduces the same defect one level down, and `notifications` carries one verdict per channel, which could then no longer be true.

⚠ **THE NOTICE IS SIZED AGAINST ITS OWN WORST CASE before anything is cut** — its length depends on the numbers printed inside it, so "reserve a fixed 60 characters" is the shape that fails at a boundary nobody tested. **That mutation broke 4 of the 11 cases**, which is how I know the property is pinned rather than described.

✅ **Five mutations, five caught:** the sender's bound removed · severity order inverted · dropped criticals no longer named · the per-line cap removed · the notice not sized for its worst case. Full suite **1,496 files / 16,610 tests green**, `tsc --noEmit` clean.

### 2026-09-10 · 🔴 Autovacuum had NEVER run on `net._http_response` because the stat that gates it read ZERO dead tuples against a true 161,390 — one 581 ms ANALYZE fixed it, and a second lever had to be cancelled · Claude Code (cloud), Trevor: "Keep going and plan on working autonomously"

**Shipped: one live `ANALYZE` (no DDL, no migration, no schedule, no data mutation) + register #75. ⚠ One manual `VACUUM` was started and CANCELLED — see below; nothing was harmed and that is verified, not assumed.**

⭐⭐ **FOUND BY CAPTURING A LIVE SATURATION WINDOW INSTEAD OF RECONSTRUCTING ONE.** At 23:02Z the instance read **34 active / 20 IO waiters**. Two `pg_statio_user_tables` snapshots **225 s** apart name the reader: **`net._http_response`, 132,617 blocks — ≈589 blocks/s, 2.8× the next table** (`wallet_moments_cache` 47,023 · `fmv_snapshots_2026` 45,727 · `sales_2026` 13,977) — **despite being only 4th by CUMULATIVE reads**, which is why no previous sweep saw it. ⓘ On a Small tier with a **22 MB/s** budget that is **≈4.6 MB/s, about a fifth of the whole instance, spent reading a table that is 95% dead space.**

⭐ **AND THE LIVE WAIT BREAKDOWN SETTLES WHAT `cron.job_run_details` CANNOT — it is IO, not a lock.** 12 sessions `IO/DataFileRead`, 9 `IPC/BufferIo` (backends queueing for the SAME buffers), **ZERO on any `Lock`/`LWLock`**. ⭐ **And `authenticator` holds 9 of the 12 IO waiters and 9 of 9 `BufferIo` — the pressure is REST-side**, which corroborates #73's wallet-backfill conclusion on a **third** instrument.

🚨 **THE MECHANISM, and it is a statistic lying rather than a query being slow.** `pg_net.ttl = 6 hours` and pruning **works** (11,036 live rows, oldest 17:08Z, newest 23:07Z). But **`n_live_tup` read 639, `n_dead_tup` read 0, `autovacuum_count` 0, `autoanalyze_count` 0, `last_autovacuum` NULL — for the table's entire life.** Autovacuum's trigger is computed FROM `n_dead_tup`, so **a stat pinned at 0 makes it unreachable by construction**: the deletes happen forever and the vacuum never does, and the TOAST extends **~1.2–2 GB/day**. `reloptions` NULL on heap and toast, so it was never disabled — just never *seen*. **8,574 MB total = 176 MB heap + 8,395 MB TOAST, holding 443 MB of live bodies (avg 41 kB).**

✅ **FIXED AND VERIFIED, FOR 581 ms.** `ANALYZE net._http_response` at **23:09:06Z** moved `n_dead_tup` **0 → 161,390**, and **autovacuum fired 43 SECONDS LATER at 23:09:49Z** (`autovacuum_count` 0 → 1), clearing all 161,390. ⭐ **The fix unblocks the estate's own maintenance rather than substituting for it** — autovacuum is throttled (`cost_delay` 2 ms) and did the work without harm.

⚠⚠ **I THEN TRIED A SECOND LEVER AND HAD TO CANCEL IT, WHICH IS THE MORE USEFUL HALF.** A manual `VACUUM (ANALYZE)` is **UNTHROTTLED**: it blew past the 60 s MCP timeout, was still in `IO/DataFileRead` at **66 s**, and drove `io_waiters` **0–2 → 6** on an instance with a documented saturation problem, in a wallet-backfill hour. **Cancelled with `pg_cancel_backend`.** ✅ **Verified no damage rather than assumed: `vacuums_running` 0 afterwards and ZERO cron failures in the 10-minute window.** **Measured costs: `ANALYZE` 580.8 ms vs manual `VACUUM` >60 s — ~100×.**

⛔ **SO THE OBVIOUS REMEDIATION IS THE WRONG ONE, and I only know that because I ran it.** Scheduling a manual vacuum here — mirroring the existing `maint-vacuum-sales-hot-partition [53 10,20 * * *]` precedent — **would reproduce exactly the IO spike I had to cancel.** If a job is needed at all it should be a scheduled **cheap `ANALYZE`**, because autovacuum itself is throttled and competent once it can see the truth.

⚠ **WHETHER A JOB IS NEEDED IS NOT YET ESTABLISHED, and the test is running.** `n_dead_tup` read 0 at 23:15Z and 238 after a manual ANALYZE — **but ANALYZE sets that value directly, so 238 may be my own measurement rather than the collector recovering.** Re-read after ~20 minutes with **no** manual ANALYZE: **climbing → autovacuum self-sustains, no job needed; frozen → a scheduled `ANALYZE` is required.**

⛔ **STILL TREVOR'S, and it is the bigger number: the existing ~8.4 GB of bloated TOAST is NOT recovered by any of this.** Plain vacuum only marks space reusable; returning it to the OS needs **`VACUUM FULL`, ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, which would block every pg_net lane** — a maintenance-window decision, not an autonomous one.

**Files:** `docs/reference/known-issues.md` (#75 new), `docs/overnight/ledger.md`, `docs/sessions/2026-09.md`.

**Revert:** nothing to revert in git beyond docs. **The DB change is an `ANALYZE`, which only refreshes statistics — it is not reversible and does not need to be.** If the resulting autovacuum activity were ever unwanted, `ALTER TABLE net._http_response SET (autovacuum_enabled = false)` would stop it — ⛔ but that restores the exact defect this item is about, so do not.

### 2026-09-10 · 🔴 The saturation bursts RECURRED on schedule, and 48 h of hourly data refutes the amplifier this estate had settled on — staggering pg_cron cannot fix it · Claude Code (cloud), Trevor: "Keep going"

**Shipped: docs only — register #73 extended. READ-ONLY. No migration, no data mutation, no schedule touched, nothing paused. The root cause is still NOT settled and the reason for shipping nothing operational is stated below.**

⭐ **The new arm found it on its first real day.** `check_pgcron_failure_rate('6 hours')` read **158 fails / 2,157 runs across 38 jobs (63 startup, 95 statement)** at 13:45Z — well over its 10-per-6h bar. That is the arm doing exactly the job it was built for: yesterday this surface was watched by nothing.

🚨 **THE BURSTS ARE A RECURRING DAILY PATTERN, NOT THE ONE-OFF SPELL #73 DESCRIBES.** `job startup timeout` lands at **09-09 12Z (10) · 13Z (66) · 18Z (59)** and again at **09-10 12Z (34) · 13Z (29)** — and at **ZERO of the other 43 hours** in the 48 h window. Same clock hours, next day.

⛔⛔ **AND THE `*/6` CLUSTERING IS REFUTED AS THE CAUSE — by measurement, against the explanation this estate had already accepted.** #73 records the amplifier as "the six-hourly heavy MV refreshes cluster at minutes 20–50 of hours 0/6/12/18; at today's runtimes they OVERLAP and exhaust the slots." **The scheduled population is IDENTICAL across all four windows** — every job in the top-20 by duration runs the same number of times at 0Z, 6Z, 12Z, 18Z (2/2/2/2, 12/12/12/12, 60/60/58/60) — **and at 0Z and 6Z that identical cluster finishes in seconds.** Same job, max duration by hour: `remap-misattributed-sales` **51 · 27 · 780 · 530 s**; `refresh-mv-pack-ev-latest` **9 · 7 · 600 · 688 s**; `refresh-topshot-pack-sales-agg` **197 · 16 · 617 · 600 s**; `backfill-pinnacle-mint-acquisitions` **57 · 22 · 869 · 212 s**. ⭐ **The variable is the HOUR, not the schedule. So staggering pg_cron cannot fix this, and any analysis that reads only `cron.job` is looking in the wrong place** — which is most of them, mine included until today.

⭐⭐ **`job startup timeout` IS A SYMPTOM, AND THE SECOND-LEVEL TRACE SHOWS WHAT IT IS A SYMPTOM OF: A MASS RELEASE.** At **09-09 12:36Z, 29 runs across 21 distinct jobs ended inside ONE MINUTE with durations spanning 0 s to 788 s.** ⚠ **A shared DURATION is a timeout; a shared INSTANT across heterogeneous durations is a global unblock** — that distinction is the whole finding. Nine long jobs (306 · 307 · 310 · 341 · 363 · 422 · 547 · 780 · 788 s) all finished between **12:36:00.867 and 12:36:12.457**, several returning `1 row` after 300–780 s — **waiting, not computing**. Five jobs launched at 12:36:04 then died with `job startup timeout` at 12:36:15–16 (11.0–11.3 s each) because the six slots were still held, and at 12:36:14 the backlog burst through at **0.1–0.5 s per job**. **Order: stall → slots stay held → launches fail → release → flood.**

⛔ **One mechanism ruled out for the price of one query: it is NOT a `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW` ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock.** All **11** active bare-refresh jobs use **`CONCURRENTLY`**, which does not block readers. Still plausible IO contributors; not the blocker. **Recorded so nobody re-runs that hunt.**

⭐ **INDEPENDENT INSTRUMENT, AND IT POINTS AWAY FROM pg_cron:** `pipeline_runs` counts by UTC hour over the same 48 h vary **3.1×** — ~1,150–1,250/h baseline against **13Z 3,559 · 18Z 3,215 · 07Z 3,064 · 01Z 2,795** — with median duration tracking it (**13Z 17,048 ms** vs ~1,200–2,000 ms). With the pg_cron population flat, **that variation belongs to the other schedulers** — cron-job.org, GHA, `vercel.json`, the residential box — the sources this file already names as invisible to a `cron.job` sweep.

⚠ **THE HYPOTHESIS IS STATED WITH ITS OWN COUNTEREXAMPLE, not without it: the bursts appear to need BOTH the cluster AND high external load.** 07Z has load and no cluster → clean; 6Z has the cluster and the lowest load → clean; 12/13Z and 18Z have both → bursts. ⛔ **But 0Z carries 2,057 runs against 12Z's 1,648 and is still clean, so run COUNT alone does not separate them.** The discriminator is more likely the COST of the concurrent work than its count, and that is **not established**. ⛔ **Nothing operational was changed: the levers are capacity (Trevor's, and there is no infra spend pre-revenue) and the external schedulers' timing, and neither should move on a hypothesis with a live counterexample in it.**

⭐⭐ **ONE HOUR LATER, THE COUNTEREXAMPLE ABOVE IS RESOLVED — and the fix was a better DENOMINATOR, not more data.** The paragraph above could not separate 0Z from 12Z because it compared TOTAL `pipeline_runs` counts. **Split by lane and it separates immediately: the load is the `wallet-backfill` family, and it is violently bursty** — runs/hour over 48 h read **13Z 1,728 · 18Z 1,636 · 07Z 1,456 · 01Z 990 · 22Z 959 · 00Z 615 · 12Z 424**, and **exactly ZERO at fourteen of the twenty-four hours**. Per-run cost inflates with it (`wallet-backfill-pinnacle` median **58,815 ms** burst vs **10,582 ms** clean; `-multicollection-complete` **194,729** vs **59,431**).

✅ **BOTH SINGLE-FACTOR CONTROLS ARE IN THE DATA, which is what makes this an interaction and not a story.** **06Z — the six-hourly cluster with ZERO wallet runs → clean. 07Z — 1,456 wallet runs with NO cluster → clean. 13Z and 18Z — both → bursts.** Either factor alone is survivable; together they exhaust the six worker slots.

⭐ **AND THE OVERLAP FALLS OUT OF THE COHORT TIMING #48 ALREADY RECORDS.** `seed-wallet-refresh` fires 12 dispatches at **07Z, 13Z, 18Z**, so **the 0Z and 6Z cohorts' work lands in the FOLLOWING hour and misses the heavies entirely**, while the 12Z heavies run **600–869 s** and are still holding slots when 13Z's flood arrives, and at 18Z the cohort (:13/:27) and the heavies (:20–:50) overlap head-on. **That is the whole of why 0Z/6Z are clean and 12/13Z/18Z are not.**

⛔ **Still nothing changed, and the reason is unchanged: a plausible mechanism is not a measurement.** ⭐ **But #48's untested cohort-spacing experiment now has a SECOND, independent reason to run — saturation rather than waste — and a cheaper first probe than the one it proposes: move EITHER side of the 18Z overlap and leave 12/13Z as the control. FALSIFIER: if 18Z's startup timeouts do not fall while 12/13Z's hold, the overlap is not the mechanism.** ⚠ **Caveat kept in view: burst-hour run COUNT may be partly an EFFECT, since #48 records ~9× re-dispatch and a higher kill rate in busy hours. The 06Z/07Z pair carries the argument, because there the 0-vs-1,456 split is SCHEDULE, not retry.**

### 2026-07-16 (Claude Code, interactive, afternoon) — night-queue Item 1 SHIPPED: `get_lock_check_batch` index-driven rewrite kills the #1 disk reader (1,522 MB/193s → 8.4 MB/119ms)

Worked the 07-16 night handoff ([docs/handoff-2026-07-16-evening-queue.md](../archive/handoffs/handoff-2026-07-16-evening-queue.md)) top item — the post-wmc-fix #1 pg_stat_statements reader. Shipped **1** (DB-only, 1 index + 1 fn rewrite), reverted 0. Pure DB; no code deploy. Ledger is the record.

- **SHIPPED — `get_lock_check_batch` index-driven rewrite** (migrations `audit_20260716_wmc_lockcheck_order_index` + `audit_20260716_get_lock_check_batch_index_driven_rewrite`). The old body window-ranked the ENTIRE stale `wallet_moments_cache` set (~2.0M rows) per call with a per-row `EXISTS(hot_wallets)` subplan in both the SELECT and the window `ORDER BY`, then `LIMIT p_limit` — measured **1,522 MB read / 193s in a single call** (historic 1,286 GB / 1,460 calls). It was the driver of the hourly IOPS-saturation windows (page-view 30s statement-timeouts + smoke pages). New body: index `idx_wmc_lockcheck_order (collection_id, lock_checked_at ASC NULLS FIRST)` (14 MB) + two index-driven arms per collection off that index — (a) fill = the p_limit stalest rows in the collection, (b) priority = the p_limit stalest rows owned by a hot wallet (472 hot addrs, materialized once) — `UNION ALL`, dedup (`bool_or` reconstructs `is_priority` with **no** per-row EXISTS), then rank priority-first/stalest-first per collection and round-robin via `ORDER BY rn, collection_id`. **Identical batch semantics** to the old body (validated pre-swap: golazos scoped old-vs-new = 44/44 rows, 0 set diff, 0 priority-flag mismatch; + composition proof — each arm capped at p_limit is sufficient because the final batch is ≤ p_limit total). **EXPLAIN (ANALYZE,BUFFERS)** unscoped/limit200: `Index Scan using idx_wmc_lockcheck_order` on both arms, **shared hit=690 read=383 (~8.4 MB) / Execution 119 ms** (was 1,522 MB / 193,000 ms → ~180× fewer reads, ~1,600× faster). Live fn verified: 200 rows / 5 collections / 0 null keys / priority-first (matches old ranking); SECDEF + ACL `postgres`+`service_role` only (no anon/authenticated). Route unchanged (still reads the same 4 out_ cols).
  - **Build note (reusable):** MCP `execute_sql` wraps multi-statement calls in a txn (→ `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` 25001); a lone-statement CONCURRENTLY avoids the txn but is still 2min-capped and one full 785 MB wmc scan already exceeds 2 min under contention → canceled → invalid 0-byte index. Built instead via `apply_migration` plain `CREATE INDEX` in a verified-idle window (active=0) guarded by `SET LOCAL lock_timeout='4s'` + `maintenance_work_mem='128MB'`; completed <2 min, `indisvalid=true`. See [[route-db-calls-inherit-8s-statement-timeout]].
  - **Revert:** `DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS public.idx_wmc_lockcheck_order;` + recreate the prior `get_lock_check_batch` body from migration history (the `WITH hot_wallets … ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY collection_id ORDER BY EXISTS(...) DESC, lock_checked_at NULLS FIRST)` window version).
  - **Target metric:** `get_lock_check_batch` drops out of the top of `pg_stat_statements` by shared_blks_read/call (≈0.9 GB/call → <0.02 GB/call); the hourly page-view statement-timeout bursts + smoke saturation windows stop; `lock-check-batch` pipeline stays ok=true.

Trevor: "get local main to stop falling behind and continuously stay synced across all mains." **Diagnosis:** the alarming "50 ahead / 50 behind" on local `main` was a **shallow-clone illusion** — web sessions clone this repo shallow (~50 deep) and start on a fresh `claude/*` branch, so the true merge-base sits below the fetch horizon and git falsely reports divergence. After `git fetch --unshallow`, local `main` was **0 ahead / 110 behind** = pure ancestor, just stale, no lost work, no conflicts. One-time fix applied live (`git branch -f main origin/main`).

- **SHIPPED (infra) — `.claude/hooks/session-start.sh` + `.claude/settings.json` (`e01575ab`).** SessionStart hook (web-only, synchronous, idempotent) runs every session: unshallows the clone so relationships compute truthfully → fast-forwards local `main` to `origin/main` with `--ff-only` (**never** clobbers genuine unpushed commits — leaves them with a notice) → checks out `main` on a clean tree (per CLAUDE.md "always work on main"). `.gitignore` narrowed from `.claude/` to un-ignore ONLY those two shared files; local `.claude/` state stays ignored. Validated: caught a live `origin/main` advance (`d2b0eab2`→`a7421ee7`) and ff'd automatically; claude/*→main checkout path + non-remote guard both pass. **NOTE for nightly pass / monitor:** `.claude/hooks/` + `.claude/settings.json` are now TRACKED files — expected, not drift. **Revert:** `git rm -r .claude/hooks .claude/settings.json` + restore `.gitignore` line 52 to `.claude/`, or `git revert e01575ab`.

Picked up `docs/handoff-2026-07-12-*` (the overnight cron-failure investigation). Shipped the one blocked code item, then verified the DB-side fixes — and found the primary one never worked.

- **SHIPPED (code) — buyer-backfill forward lane bound to 2025+ (`44d741e`, prod `dpl_CEZHf4k6...` READY).** Added `.gte("sold_at", '2025-01-01')` to the forward null-buyer select in `app/api/admin/backfill-topshot-buyers/route.ts` (uses existing `HIST_WINDOW_END`) + `app/api/admin/backfill-allday-buyers/route.ts` (new `FORWARD_WINDOW_START` const).
